title: Degenerative Disc Changes in Adjacent Segments Following Spinal Trauma with Spondylodesis A clinical, radiological, single-center, retrospective study
summary:
Degeneration and disease of spinal segments adjacent to a cervical or thoracolumbar spinal fusion (spondylodesis) are well-known postoperative problems when the primary indication for surgery is a degenerative spinal condition.

However, it remains unclear whether this problem represents a continuation of the individual's natural progression of intervertebral disc degeneration (chondrosis) or whether it is an iatrogenically induced phenomenon following spinal fusion, for example due to increased and potentially pathological mechanical stress on the adjacent segments.

The reason for this uncertainty is that most of the current literature on this topic does not adequately address: (a) the pre-existing degeneration (chondrosis/spondylosis) of adjacent segments before surgery, and (b) the fact that most follow-up studies have been conducted in patients who underwent surgery for degenerative disc disease. Furthermore, Hilibrand et al. demonstrated that the rate of symptomatic adjacent segment degeneration was actually higher in patients who underwent single-level fusion compared with those who underwent multi-level fusion. This finding raises the question of whether adjacent segment degeneration is truly an iatrogenic phenomenon.

While adjacent segment degeneration is undoubtedly a significant issue in patients with degenerative spinal disorders, the situation may differ in the trauma population, as these patients are less likely to have suffered from a pre-existing symptomatic degenerative disc disease prior to injury. Therefore, a follow-up study comparing adjacent segment degeneration (ASD) rates in patients who underwent spinal fusion (a) following vertebral trauma and (b) for pre-existing degenerative disc disease appears warranted in order to better understand the etiology of adjacent segment degeneration and disease.

The aim of this study is therefore to determine the impact of cervical and thoracolumbar spinal fusion procedures on the incidence of adjacent segment degeneration and disease following acute traumatic spinal injury in patients without evidence of pre-existing chondrosis or spondylosis.

We hypothesize that adjacent segment degeneration is primarily related to an individual's predisposition to degenerative disc disease and its natural progression. Consequently, patients who undergo cervical or thoracolumbar spinal fusion for acute traumatic injuries of the cervical, thoracic, or lumbar spine, without evidence of pre-existing spondylosis, will demonstrate a lower rate of postoperative symptomatic adjacent segment degeneration compared with patients who undergo the same surgical procedure for degenerative spinal conditions.

Secondary outcome measures include surgical techniques used, follow-up intervals, and other treatment-related complications such as infection, implant loosening, implant failure, and loss of correction.

In this retrospective study, available radiographic, CT, and MRI imaging studies, together with digital medical records of patients treated for traumatic injuries of the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine, will be reviewed over the longest possible follow-up period. The incidence of radiologically detected and/or clinically symptomatic degenerative changes and diseases of adjacent spinal segments will be determined and compared.

interventions.name: Patients over the age of 18 who are capable of giving informed consent and who, over a 15-year period (2010–2025), underwent instrumented cervical or thoracolumbar spondylodesis on the subaxial cervical spine between C3 and C7, the thoracic and lumbar spine, including the lumbosacral junction betwee
Patients who meet the above criteria and who have undergone surgery for a degenerative spinal condition.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
All patients over the age of 18 who are capable of giving informed consent and who, over a 15-year period (2010–2025), underwent instrumented cervical or thoracolumbar spondylodesis on the subaxial cervical spine between C3 and C7, the thoracic and lumbar spine, including the lumbosacral junction between T1 and S1, due to an acute traumatic indication (fractures/dislocations), will be included in the study.
Exclusion criteria:
Patients who have undergone cervical or thoracolumbar spondylodesis due to infectious or tumor-related conditions are excluded.
